title: Primary Aldosteronism: Resistant Hypertension Is a Diagnostic Clue
bottomLine: Primary aldosteronism is a treatable cause of hypertension that should be considered especially with resistant hypertension, unexplained spontaneous or marked diuretic-induced hypokalemia, or hypertension with an adrenal adenoma. Screen with aldosterone and renin under an interpretable medication and physiologic context, then confirm and localize through an endocrine/hypertension pathway rather than diagnosing from potassium alone.
recognize: Many patients with primary aldosteronism are normokalemic, so normal potassium does not exclude the diagnosis.
Suppressed renin with inappropriately high aldosterone raises suspicion after accounting for medications, sodium status and potassium.
differentiate: Diuretic use, gastrointestinal losses and magnesium deficiency can cause hypokalemia without autonomous aldosterone secretion.
Renovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, obstructive sleep apnea, thyroid disease, medications and substances are other secondary or aggravating causes of difficult hypertension.
assessment: Confirm true resistant hypertension with standardized and out-of-office blood pressure data, adherence assessment, medication review and evaluation for white-coat effect before labelling treatment failure.
Review potassium, renal function, licorice/supplement exposure and medications that can distort aldosterone-renin interpretation; ask about sleep apnea and other secondary-hypertension clues.
workup: Hypertension Canada recommends aldosterone plus renin assessment for screening in appropriate patients; correct clinically important hypokalemia and follow assay/local protocol preparation because several medications alter test interpretation.

A positive screening pattern requires confirmatory evaluation for autonomous aldosterone secretion when indicated, followed by localization; CT alone does not reliably prove which adrenal gland is functionally responsible.
When a surgical candidate has a definite adrenal mass and confirmed primary aldosteronism, adrenal venous sampling is generally used in experienced centres to determine lateralization.
management: Unilateral surgically correctable disease is managed through specialist adrenal evaluation; bilateral or nonsurgical disease is commonly treated with mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade plus cardiovascular risk management.
Continue evidence-based hypertension treatment while the secondary-cause workup proceeds rather than withholding necessary blood-pressure control.
medicationSafety: Spironolactone and eplerenone can cause hyperkalemia and kidney-function changes; monitor potassium and creatinine after initiation and dose changes.
Starting spironolactone before planned aldosterone-renin testing can interfere with interpretation, so coordinate medication changes rather than stopping antihypertensives unsafely.
redFlags: Severe hypertension with acute target-organ injury
Severe hypokalemia with arrhythmia or weakness
Adrenal mass with features suggesting another functional tumour or malignancy
counselling: Explain that finding primary aldosteronism matters because targeted therapy may improve blood pressure and reduce excess cardiovascular risk beyond simply adding another nonspecific antihypertensive.
followUp: Track blood pressure, potassium, kidney function and treatment adverse effects; specialist follow-up determines biochemical response and surgical or medical long-term strategy.
examTrap: Ruling out primary aldosteronism because the potassium is normal, or ordering a CT first and declaring an incidental adrenal nodule to be the cause without biochemical confirmation.
oneLinePearl: Resistant hypertension can be an aldosterone problem even when potassium is normal.
sourceBasis: Hypertension Canada comprehensive guidance: Assessment for Endocrine Hypertension

title: Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma: Catecholamine Clues Before Imaging
bottomLine: Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma are uncommon but dangerous catecholamine-secreting tumours. Screen when the phenotype fits—paroxysmal or severe/labile resistant hypertension, compatible catecholamine symptoms, an adrenal incidentaloma, a suggestive trigger pattern, or hereditary predisposition—and establish biochemical evidence before localization imaging whenever the patient is stable enough for the standard pathway.
recognize: Episodic headache, palpitations, sweating, pallor, tremor or panic-like spells with marked blood-pressure variability raise suspicion, but no single symptom triad is diagnostic.
Hypertension may be sustained or paroxysmal; an adrenal incidentaloma can be the first clue in an otherwise less dramatic presentation.
differentiate: Panic disorder, hyperthyroidism, stimulant or decongestant use, withdrawal states, obstructive sleep apnea, hypoglycemia and other causes of sympathetic activation can mimic catecholamine excess.
A nonspecific adrenal nodule is common and does not prove pheochromocytoma without biochemical evaluation.
assessment: Document attack timing, blood-pressure pattern, headache/palpitations/sweating, medication and substance triggers, family history and syndromic features such as MEN2, VHL or NF1.
Ask whether episodes occur with surgery, anesthesia, abdominal pressure, urination or medications that can precipitate catecholamine release.
workup: Use recommended biochemical screening such as plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines through an appropriate protocol; pre-analytic conditions and interfering drugs matter when interpreting borderline results.

Hypertension Canada recommends specialist referral when suspicion is strong, particularly after a positive biochemical screen; localization imaging follows biochemical evidence in the standard stable pathway.
management: Confirmed disease requires specialist endocrine, hypertension, anesthesia and surgical planning; preoperative catecholamine control is protocolized and should not be improvised in routine ambulatory care.
A catecholamine crisis with severe hypertension and acute organ injury requires emergency monitored management.
medicationSafety: Do not give an isolated beta blocker before adequate alpha-adrenergic blockade in confirmed/suspected catecholamine-secreting tumour management because unopposed alpha stimulation can worsen vasoconstriction and hypertension.
Review sympathomimetics, stimulants, MAO-related interactions and other medications that may provoke symptoms or interfere with biochemical testing.
redFlags: Chest pain, pulmonary edema or stress cardiomyopathy
Shock or marked blood-pressure instability during a suspected catecholamine crisis
counselling: Explain that a positive screen does not automatically mean cancer and that hereditary assessment may be recommended because a meaningful proportion of these tumours have genetic associations.
followUp: After definitive treatment, long-term biochemical and clinical surveillance is individualized by tumour and genetic risk; coordinate genetics when indicated.
examTrap: Ordering adrenal imaging for episodic hypertension before biochemical evaluation, or treating tachycardia with beta blockade alone when pheochromocytoma is strongly suspected.
oneLinePearl: Catecholamine tumour: prove secretion, then localize—and never forget the alpha-before-beta safety principle.
sourceBasis: Hypertension Canada comprehensive guidance: Assessment for Endocrine Hypertension
